sections.text:
Samspuchari de temporum rationibus.
Herm. Useneri beneficio qui exemplar suum accurate descriptum passimque
correctum e scriniis depromptum ornatissimis liberaliter nobiscum communica-
vit, factum est ut hoc Persarum scientiae specimen proferre nobis liceret.
Σαμψουχαρής vel rectius Σάμψ πουχαρής cui hoc opus a graeco interprete tribui-
tur, est Sams Bukharensis (Šams Aldin al Bukhârî ?) astronomus qui saeculo XIII
floruisse videtur. (Cf. Usener, Ad historiam astronomiae symbola, Bonn, 1876,
p. 15, n. d et 22 sq.). — Commentaria eorum quae edimus similia in principio
operum orientalium astronomiae vel historiae scriptorum non raro inveniuntur
velut apud Alfergani (Elementa astronomica, ed. Golius, 1669) et Albîrûnî (Chrono-
logy of ancient. nations, ed. Sachau, 1879) virum eximiae doctrinae et Bukharensi
isto multo praestantiorem. — Interpretis graecae linguae imperiti stylum barba-
rum corrigere nolui. Praemonere sufficiat verba χρόνος (annus) et καιρός (tempus)
sicut in sermone vulgari accipienda esse, ἔτος pro ἔτων περίοδος usurpari et τὸν
ψῆφον perpetuo dici.
sections.en:
Samspuchari on the reckoning of times.
By the kindness of Herm. Usener, who generously communicated to us his copy, accurately transcribed and corrected here and there, drawn from his most elegant files, it has come about that we are permitted to present this specimen of Persian science.
Sampsouchares, or more correctly Samps pouchares, to whom this work is attributed by the Greek translator, is Sams of Bukhara (Šams Aldin al Bukhârî?), an astronomer who seems to have flourished in the 13th century. (Cf. Usener, Ad historiam astronomiae symbola, Bonn, 1876, p. 15, n. d and 22 sq.). — Commentaries similar to those which we publish are not rarely found at the beginning of the works of oriental writers on astronomy or history, as in Alfergani (Elementa astronomica, ed. Golius, 1669) and Albîrûnî (Chronology of ancient nations, ed. Sachau, 1879), a man of outstanding learning and much superior to that Bukharian. — I have been unwilling to correct the barbarous style of the translator, who was unskilled in the Greek language. Let it suffice to warn in advance that the words χρόνος (year) and καιρός (time) are to be taken as in common speech, that ἔτος is used for ἔτων περίοδος, and that τὸν ψῆφον is said perpetually.

sections.en:
Here it is intended to be told how every nation reckons times: Persians, Christians, Hebrews, Idolaters, Hittites, astronomers, Indians.
The astronomers properly reckon the year from the sun, numbering the beginning of the year from there, from the rising of the sun.
But the Persians number the years from the moon, and they reckon the first year from Muharram, and they calculate the beginning of their month from that, when they see the new moon.
The Christians number the years from the sun; but this is not properly so, because one of their years is 365 days and a quarter, and it has been said that this year of the sun is not completed; for something is lacking from the quarter; but they altogether reckon this year on this account, inasmuch as the year of the sun is very much of the complete one; and they place the beginning of their year at the middle of Libra; but they also calculate the beginning of their months from September.

summary.headline: Samspuchares on Reckoning Times
summary.text: Samspuchares’ treatise on reckoning times is introduced as a specimen of Persian science, attributed to Sams of Bukhara and discussed alongside Alfergani and Albîrûnî. The opening diagnosis compares how Persians, Christians, Hebrews, Idolaters, Hittites, astronomers, and Indians reckon years, including Muharram, the solar year, Libra, and September.
